title: What a Runtime Provides
summary: A language runtime is everything running under your program while it runs — not just "the interpreter." See the services it provides, where the compiler's job ends and the runtime's begins, and why that split has a real startup-time cost.

slides.markdown:
Ask most engineers what "the runtime" is and you'll hear "the interpreter" or "the thing that runs the bytecode." That's the visible tenth of it.

A **runtime** is the layer of software that is actively working underneath your program from the moment it starts to the moment it exits — managing memory, checking types, catching exceptions, and providing the standard library your code calls into. It sits between your compiled/interpreted program and the operating system.

This group walks through what runtimes do (this topic), the bytecode formats they execute, how they get native speed via JIT compilation, and deep dives into the JVM, CLR, V8, and CPython. Understanding the runtime is what separates "I can write Java" from "I understand what happens when `java Main` runs."

slides.subTitle: Four jobs running under your code
slides.markdown:
A managed runtime typically provides four load-bearing services, all invisible until they fail:

- **Memory management** — allocating objects and reclaiming ones nothing references anymore (see `memory-gc` for the mechanics).
- **Type and safety enforcement** — checking that a cast is legal, an array index is in bounds, a null isn't dereferenced — at run time, because the compiler couldn't prove it statically.
- **Standard library and I/O** — the actual code behind `System.out.println` or `open()`, plus the glue that talks to the OS's file and network syscalls.
- **Exception/error handling** — unwinding the call stack, running `finally` blocks, and delivering a stack trace when something goes wrong.

None of these are "the language." They're services the runtime supplies so the language doesn't have to re-implement them per program.

Layer it from the bottom up: hardware, then the operating system, then the runtime, then your running program on top. Your code never talks to the OS directly — every syscall, every memory allocation, every thread creation is mediated by the runtime layer.

That mediation is the whole value proposition: your Java code doesn't know if it's on Linux or Windows because the JVM absorbed that difference underneath it.

slides.subTitle: Where the line is drawn
slides.markdown:
The compiler and the runtime split the work of "make this program correct and fast," and the split point matters for debugging:

| Question | Compiler answers | Runtime answers |
|---|---|---|
| Is this syntax valid? | Yes | — |
| Does this type-check statically? | Yes (where the type system allows) | Residual checks it couldn't prove |
| Will this array index be in bounds? | Rarely provable | Checked every access |
| When does this object's memory get freed? | Never — no visibility into runtime lifetimes | Yes, via the GC |
| Which method does this virtual call resolve to? | Narrows candidates | Resolves the actual target, sometimes per-call |

A `NullPointerException` or `IndexOutOfBoundsException` at 2am is a runtime check firing — the compiler let the code through because it genuinely couldn't rule the case out.

slides.sectionTitle: Managed runtimes vs no separate runtime
slides.markdown:
Not every language pays for a runtime layer the same way:

- **Managed runtimes** (JVM, CLR, V8, CPython's interpreter) provide GC, bytecode execution, and safety checks as a continuously-running service alongside your program. You gain memory safety and portability; you pay in startup cost, memory footprint, and a layer of indirection.
- **"No separate runtime" languages** (C, and largely Rust/Go — see `ahead-of-time-compilation-and-native-images` later in this group) compile straight to a native binary. There's still a small runtime shim (C's `libc` startup code, Go's scheduler), but there's no persistent VM interpreting anything while your program runs.

The trade isn't "managed is slow, native is fast" — it's safety, portability, and productivity against startup latency and footprint. A JVM microservice with a 300ms cold start and a Go binary with a 5ms cold start are both valid choices for different constraints.

slides.sectionTitle: Why runtime-backed apps are slow to start
slides.subTitle: Startup cost and footprint
slides.markdown:
Before your `main` method runs a single line, a managed runtime has already done real work:

- Loaded and verified its own core classes (the JVM's bootstrap classloader loading `java.lang.*` before it can even load *your* class).
- Initialized the garbage collector's heap regions.
- Set up the interpreter loop and, on the JVM/CLR, the JIT infrastructure that will later kick in (`just-in-time-compilation`).

That's why a "hello world" JVM program can take 100–300ms to print, while the equivalent C binary prints in single-digit milliseconds. It's not that Java is slow — it's that the runtime is doing setup work a native binary skips entirely. This is exactly the cost `ahead-of-time-compilation-and-native-images` and `the-jvm-deep-dive`'s tiered JIT both exist to reduce.

slides.subTitle: "This language is slow"
slides.markdown:
A common misdiagnosis: benchmarking a managed language for 50ms, seeing a bad number, and concluding "this language is slow."

What's usually happening is a **runtime warm-up effect**, not a language property:

- The JIT hasn't identified hot methods yet, so code is still running interpreted (`just-in-time-compilation`).
- Classes are still being lazily loaded and linked on first use.
- The GC hasn't settled into a steady-state heap size and is still resizing.

Run the same benchmark for 10 seconds instead of 50ms and the numbers often change by 10x. This is why serious benchmarks report warmed-up throughput, not the first call — and why "my Lambda is slow" is frequently a cold-start problem, not an algorithm problem.

slides.sectionTitle: The standard library is part of the runtime
slides.markdown:
It's easy to think of "the language" as syntax and "the runtime" as an implementation detail underneath it, but a huge amount of what you use daily lives in the runtime's standard library — code shipped and versioned with the runtime itself, not your program.

This is why a JVM upgrade can change behavior without you touching your code: `HashMap`'s internals, `String`'s interning strategy, and `ArrayList`'s growth factor are all runtime-owned. It's also why cross-runtime portability claims ("Python code runs anywhere") quietly assume the *same* standard library version is present — a script using a Python 3.11-only stdlib feature doesn't run on a 3.8 runtime, even though the language syntax is compatible.

slides.sectionTitle: What's actually running when you launch a program
slides.markdown:
Walk through `java Main`, end to end, and the runtime's fingerprints are everywhere:

1. The OS loads the `java` executable, which is itself a small native launcher.
2. That launcher starts the JVM, which initializes its heap, thread model, and bootstrap classloader.
3. The bootstrap classloader loads core JDK classes, then your application classloader loads `Main.class`.
4. Class linking/verification runs (bytecode gets checked for safety before a single instruction executes).
5. `main` finally starts, running interpreted at first.

Every one of those steps is the runtime, not the OS and not your code. A senior answer to "what's running when you launch a Java program" names these phases instead of jumping straight to "the JVM interprets bytecode."

- **`dynamic-language-runtimes-v8-and-cpython`** — what changes when the *language* is dynamically typed.
